name: Mordecai
bio:
Mordecai, a Benjamite descended from Kish, had been carried into exile from Jerusalem with King Jeconiah. Living in Susa, he raised his orphaned cousin Hadassah, also called Esther, as his own daughter. When King Ahasuerus searched his empire for a new queen, Esther was among the young women brought to the palace; Mordecai instructed her not to reveal her Jewish identity, and he kept daily watch outside the harem to learn how she fared. After Esther became queen, Mordecai, now serving at the king's gate, overheard two chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, plotting to assassinate the king; he reported it through Esther, the plotters were hanged, and the event was recorded in the royal chronicles (Esther 2:5-23). His pivotal role opposing Haman is told in detail in the chapters ahead. When Haman was promoted above all other officials and demanded reverence, Mordecai alone refused to bow, revealing he was a Jew; Haman's fury at this led him to plot the destruction of all Jews in the empire (Esther 3:1-6).

 When Mordecai learned of Haman's decree, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourned bitterly in the city; through the chamberlain Hatach, he sent Esther a copy of the decree and urged her to plead with the king for her people. When Esther hesitated, fearing death for approaching the king unsummoned, Mordecai warned her that she would not escape the coming destruction either, and famously asked whether she had come to her royal position for exactly this moment; Esther then resolved to go to the king, risking her life, and asked Mordecai to have the Jews of Susa fast for her three days (Esther 4:1-17). Haman's fury that Mordecai still would not bow or rise for him, despite his royal favor and invitation to Esther's banquets, led him, on his wife Zeresh's advice, to build a gallows intending to have Mordecai hanged on it (Esther 5:9-14).

 That same night, the sleepless king had the court chronicles read to him and was reminded that Mordecai had never been rewarded for exposing the chamberlains' assassination plot. Ahasuerus asked Haman, who had come to request Mordecai's execution, what should be done for a man the king wished to honor; unknowingly describing his own enemy's reward, Haman proposed royal robes, the king's horse, and a procession through the city — which the king then ordered him to carry out for Mordecai himself. Haman led Mordecai through the streets proclaiming his honor, then went home humiliated, while his wife Zeresh and his advisors warned him that he could not prevail against a Jew before whom he had already begun to fall (Esther 6:1-13).

 The king gave Haman's estate to Esther and, learning of Mordecai's relationship to her, brought him before him and gave him the signet ring once taken from Haman; Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman's household. When Esther pleaded further for her people, the king let Mordecai draft a new decree in his name, sealed with the royal ring, granting Jews throughout the empire the right to defend themselves and strike back against any who attacked them on the day appointed for their destruction. Mordecai's decree went out by swift couriers, and he himself emerged in royal blue, white, and purple with a great gold crown, to the city's rejoicing (Esther 8:1-17).

 On the day appointed for their destruction, the Jews instead struck down their enemies throughout the empire, aided by officials who feared the now-powerful Mordecai; in Susa they killed Haman's ten sons and five hundred others, and at Esther's request the king let the killing continue there a second day and had Haman's sons' bodies hanged. Mordecai then wrote to all the Jews establishing the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as Purim, an annual festival of feasting, joy, and gift-giving to commemorate their deliverance from Haman's plot; Esther joined him in writing a second letter with full authority to confirm the observance for all generations (Esther 9:1-10:3). Mordecai rose to become second only to King Ahasuerus himself, great among the Jews and well regarded by his people, always seeking their welfare and speaking peace to his countrymen (Esther 10:1-3).
